newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to "respond appropriately" to Iraqi flights.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to "respond appropriately" to Iraqi flights.

text.p: The White House on Monday urged Iraq to reconsider its decision to send helicopters to pick up Iraqi Moslem pilgrims from the Saudi border despite a U.S. and allied ban on flights by Iraq in the area, adding that it would "respond appropriately" to any such flights.

"We certainly recognise the significance of the haj but there are other means and procedures available for the transportation of haj pilgrims," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said, referring to the annual pilgrimage to Mecca.

"We would encourage the government of Iraq to meet its obligations under U.N. Security Council resolutions and we will monitor carefully any potential violations of the no-fly zone," he told reporters. "We will respond appropriately but we're not going to shoot down civilian helicopters."

The Iraqi News Agency reported on Monday that Iraq had decided to send helicopters to pick up Moslem pilgrims from the Saudi border in the south despite a U.S. and allied ban on flights by Iraq in the area.

Defence Secretary William Cohen said Iraq cannot dictate or flaunt no-fly rules by arbitrarily sending helicopters to pick up the pilgrims but it may be eligible for a humanitarian exemption allowing the flights if it follows proper procedure.
"The Iraqis are in no position to give any kind of dictates to the American people or to NATO or to the United Nations," Cohen told reporters.
"I think that obviously when there are humanitarian issues involved that we'd be most receptive, the United Nations would be receptive," Cohen said.

"There are rules that have to be complied with. There are requests for permission for exemptions. This may be one of them," he said. "But they're not in any positon to be simply flaunting the rules on their terms."

The Iraqi News Agency said the decision was announced after a meeting of Iraqi leaders headed by President Saddam Hussein in which they warned the United States against any attempt to intercept the helicopters. "Any American practice threatening the safety of the helicopters and the pilgrims will be met with an appropriate action," it said, quoting an authoritative source.
Spokesmen for allied forces patrolling the no-fly zone were not immediately available to comment.

Iraq flew a civilian plane to Saudi Arabia on April 9 carrying 104 elderly and sick pilgrims to Mecca for the haj pilgrimage despite U.N. sanctions imposed after Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait. The plane returned home the same day.
The U.N. Security Council issued a statement calling on Iraq not to fly more planes without its consent but stopped short of regarding the flight as a breach of the embargo.
